consensus_summary: Cedar (esp. of Lebanon) primarily symbolizes strength, majesty, enduring stature, and the flourishing of the righteous under God; the same height/grandeur commonly serves as a counter-image of human pride and worldly power that God fells, with further minority associations to messianic planting, temple purity, and cleansing rites.
book_summary: Cedar is a towering power of great height and majesty; Assyria, the house of David, and the righteous may each bear the figure, so that the cedar signifies stature rather than any one fixed identity.
book_core_identification: towering stature/height/majesty as such (no fixed identity)
boundary_disagreement: Consensus privileges the positive righteous-flourishing sense as primary and treats pride/messianic uses as secondary alternatives; the book refuses any fixed primary identity and places Assyria, Davidic house, and righteous on equal footing under the single category of stature.
rationale: Both identify the same underlying qualities (height, majesty, power) and the same biblical referents (righteous via Ps 92, Assyria via Ezek 31, Davidic/messianic via Ezek 17, lofty things judged via Isa 2). The book simply elevates the shared quality of stature into the sole core and explicitly denies a settled single identity, thereby broadening and re-ranking what the consensus presents as a primary-plus-alternatives structure without replacing the referent or excluding cases.
strongest_objection: Consensus sources regularly anchor the primary sense in Ps 92:12 and treat the pride reading as prophetic counterpoint rather than co-equal, so the book's flat denial of fixed identity may understate that conventional ranking.
